title: FNAF 2 Jumpscare
blurb: Five Nights at Freddy's 2 doubled the animatronics and removed the doors, which is another way of saying it doubled the screaming. This is what arrives when the Freddy mask goes on half a second too late: a distorted, throat-shredding blast that owes as much to deliberate audio clipping as it does to sound design. The harshness is the entire point — your brain registers it as damage before it registers it as a jumpscare, which is why the clip still works on people who have seen it a hundred times. Headphone users, consider yourselves warned.
origin: The animatronic jumpscare scream from Five Nights at Freddy's 2 (2014).

title: FNAF 3 Jumpscare
blurb: By the third game there was only one real animatronic left, and Springtrap did not need any help. The FNAF 3 jumpscare is drier and more mechanical than its predecessors — less shriek, more the awful lurching of a suit that has something inside it. Fans argue endlessly over which scream in the series is worst, and this one wins on atmosphere rather than volume: you spend the entire night chasing phantom noises and audio errors before it finally lands. Reach for it when you want creeping dread instead of a cheap pop.
origin: Springtrap's jumpscare from Five Nights at Freddy's 3 (2015).

title: FNAF 6 Jumpscare
blurb: Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria Simulator spent about four minutes pretending to be a cheerful tycoon game before revealing what it actually was. Here is the payoff: the salvage-room jumpscare that waits for anyone who kept clicking salvage instead of toss for the extra cash. Greed is the whole mechanic and this sound is the invoice. It's noticeably cleaner and better mixed than the lo-fi screeches of the 2014 originals, which somehow makes it more unpleasant, because you can hear exactly what is happening to you.
origin: The salvage jumpscare from Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria Simulator (FNAF 6, 2017).

title: FNAF 6 AM
blurb: Six in the morning: the two sweetest words in Five Nights at Freddy's. The cheer, the bell chime and the little rising jingle that together mean you survived the shift and get to add another four dollars and change to your paycheque. For anyone who played the original in 2014 this is genuine Pavlovian relief — the sound of the animatronics powering down and your heart rate following them. Excellent for marking the end of anything unbearable: a shift, an exam, a meeting that should have been an email.
origin: The 6 AM survival chime from Five Nights at Freddy's.

title: FNAF Phone Guy Call
blurb: Phone Guy is the reason anybody understands what is going on in Five Nights at Freddy's. Every night opens with his crackly, aggressively casual voicemail explaining that the animatronics do get a bit quirky after hours, that they may mistake you for an endoskeleton, and that all of this is completely normal per company policy. The gap between his relaxed tone and what he is actually describing is the funniest writing in the series — and makes his eventual fate the franchise's first real gut-punch. Play it when you need to deliver terrible news breezily.
origin: Phone Guy's night-one voicemail from Five Nights at Freddy's (2014).

title: Freddy Fazbear Laugh
blurb: For most of the first game Freddy doesn't chase you. He just laughs — a slow, echoing, unmistakably animatronic chuckle that drifts down the hallway and tells you he has moved somewhere you cannot currently see. It is the game's finest piece of psychological design: a sound with no image attached, arriving on no schedule, meaning nothing good. Veterans of the 2014 original still flinch at it a decade later. Drop it into a Discord call when somebody goes quiet for slightly too long.
origin: Freddy Fazbear's roaming laugh from Five Nights at Freddy's.

title: Balloon Boy Hello
blurb: Two cheerful syllables from the most hated character in Five Nights at Freddy's. Balloon Boy doesn't kill you; he sneaks into the office, disables your torch, and then giggles at you in the dark while Foxy handles the rest. That squeaky little greeting is the exact moment you realise the run is finished, which is why the fandom has spent a decade treating a small plastic child as a war criminal. Perfect for announcing yourself somewhere you are absolutely not welcome.
origin: Balloon Boy's greeting from Five Nights at Freddy's 2.

title: FNAF Puppet Music Box
blurb: The Puppet's music box plays a wound-down rendition of My Grandfather's Clock, and you have to keep winding it, forever, while juggling four other things at once. FNAF 2 built an entire anxiety mechanic out of a lullaby: let the tune run down and the box pops open, and nothing that emerges is friendly. Slowing music boxes are already unsettling by default; this one is load-bearing. It has since become shorthand across horror edits for something bad approaching that you have no way to stop.
origin: The Puppet's wind-up music box from Five Nights at Freddy's 2.

title: Connection Terminated
blurb: "Connection terminated. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Elizabeth..." — the opening of William Afton's monologue in Sister Location, delivered in a calm, fatherly register that makes it considerably worse. It is the most quoted piece of dialogue in the entire franchise, endlessly remixed into edits and intros, and it marks the moment FNAF stopped being scattered newspaper clippings and started being a story about a father and his daughter. Play it to cut somebody off mid-sentence with maximum theatre.
origin: William Afton's line from Five Nights at Freddy's: Sister Location (2016).

title: Is That Freddy Fazbear?
blurb: A line born entirely in the meme layer around Five Nights at Freddy's rather than in the games themselves: breathless, over-excited recognition of a bear. It sounds like a child spotting merchandise in a shop window, and it became a running joke about how thoroughly Freddy escaped his own franchise — into films, plush toys, cereal boxes and every school playground on earth. Use it any time something extremely recognisable walks into frame and somebody has to point it out.
origin: A FNAF fan-meme line about spotting Freddy Fazbear.

title: Doors Rush
blurb: If you have played Roblox Doors, this sound owns a small piece of your nervous system. The lights flicker, a screech builds, and you have roughly one second to get inside a wardrobe before Rush tears down the corridor at a speed no wardrobe should reasonably survive. It is the defining audio cue of the biggest horror game on Roblox and the reason "GET IN THE CLOSET" gets screamed in voice chats worldwide. Played cold, it still makes veteran players lunge for cover.
origin: Rush's approach cue from Roblox Doors (LSPLASH, 2022).

title: Doors Ambush
blurb: Ambush is Rush's crueller sibling: same corridor, same desperate dash for the wardrobe, except this one comes back. Repeatedly. The cue was designed to sound close enough to Rush's that you cannot immediately tell which entity you are dealing with, so the real mind-game is whether you dare step out after the first pass. Doors players have developed genuine superstitions about counting them. As a soundboard button it excels at false alarms: play it, let everyone relax, then play it again.
origin: Ambush's repeated-pass cue from Roblox Doors.

title: Doors Seek Chase
blurb: The Seek chase is where Roblox Doors stops being a hide-and-hold game and turns into a full sprint through collapsing hallways, and this frantic, driving theme is what carries it. Every choice in the mix exists to make you panic and misjudge a doorway: the tempo, the low end, the sense that the track is running slightly ahead of your feet. It is the most-clipped moment in the game and a genuinely accomplished piece of composition for a free Roblox title.
origin: The Seek chase sequence music from Roblox Doors.

title: Doors Screech Giggle
blurb: A small giggle in the dark means Screech has spawned somewhere behind you and you have about a second to spin round and look straight at it. Get it right and you are rewarded; get it wrong and you take damage you almost certainly cannot afford. Roblox Doors is full of clever audio design, but this is its sharpest trick — one sound that is simultaneously the threat and the solution. Play it near anyone wearing headphones and watch their head snap round on reflex.
origin: Screech's giggle cue from Roblox Doors.

title: c00lkidd Intro
blurb: c00lkidd started life as a Roblox exploiter legend and ended up as a playable killer in Forsaken, which is an extremely Roblox career trajectory. The intro sting is pure gremlin energy — chaotic, gleeful, deliberately childish — and it captures the character exactly: not a monster so much as a menace having the time of his life at everyone else's expense. Forsaken clips turned it into a soundboard staple within weeks. Play it when you enter a voice channel fully intending to cause problems.
origin: c00lkidd's intro sting from the Roblox game Forsaken.

title: c00lkidd Gotcha
blurb: "Gotcha!" — the line every Forsaken survivor learns to dread, chirped in that unbothered sing-song way that makes losing feel personal rather than mechanical. c00lkidd's whole design is that he refuses to take the horror seriously, and neither should you, right up until the moment he is on top of you. The clip travelled far beyond the game because it works as an audio full-stop for any prank, ambush or reveal. Use it the instant somebody falls for something.
origin: c00lkidd's catch line from the Roblox game Forsaken.

title: Roblox Gravity Coil
blurb: The springy, cartoonish boing of the Gravity Coil — the gear that let a whole generation of Roblox players float across obbies as though someone had quietly unplugged physics. It is one of the platform's oldest surviving sounds and instantly nostalgic for anybody who spent 2012 in a free-model showcase game hunting for a coil somebody had left lying around. Short, silly and very satisfying: it works as a jump cue in edits or as a punchline for anyone who trips over nothing.
origin: The Gravity Coil gear sound from Roblox.

title: Roblox Cry
blurb: The default Roblox crying sound: a small, tinny, oddly heartbreaking sob that has soundtracked a million staged blocky tragedies. Roblox roleplay servers effectively run on this clip — it is the entire emotional range of a genre compressed into two seconds of compressed audio. Deployed ironically it becomes devastating, which is precisely how the internet uses it. Play it over minor inconveniences, dropped chips, and losses of absolutely no consequence whatsoever.
origin: The stock crying emote sound used across Roblox games.

title: Gojo Domain Expansion
blurb: "Domain Expansion: Unlimited Void." Gojo Satoru's technique doesn't really attack you — it hands your brain infinite information at once and lets it fail on its own terms. The audio cue, that swelling hollow rush before everything goes completely still, became instant shorthand across anime edits for somebody about to be comprehensively outclassed. Jujutsu Kaisen gave the internet plenty of catchphrases, but this is the one people actually reach for when they want to declare an argument finished.
origin: Gojo Satoru's Unlimited Void domain from Jujutsu Kaisen.

title: Sukuna Domain Expansion
blurb: Malevolent Shrine is the nastiest domain in Jujutsu Kaisen precisely because it has no barrier — Sukuna simply lets it spill across everything nearby, and Shibuya has still not recovered. Where Gojo's domain sounds like a vacuum opening, this one sounds like a blade being drawn slowly. Anime edit accounts have since bolted the cue onto everything from basketball highlights to exam-results reaction videos. Play it at the exact moment somebody stops holding back.
origin: Ryomen Sukuna's Malevolent Shrine domain from Jujutsu Kaisen.

title: Ora Ora Ora
blurb: "ORA ORA ORA ORA ORA!" — Star Platinum's rush barrage from JoJo's Bizarre Adventure, and one of the most imitated vocal tics in all of anime. The joke and the appeal are the same thing: it is one syllable, repeated, delivered with absolutely maximum conviction, for as long as the fight requires. JoJo turned onomatopoeia into a personality trait and this is the peak of it. Ideal for edits, for pretending to beat somebody up over voice chat, or for punctuating a genuinely spectacular combo.
origin: Jotaro Kujo's Star Platinum barrage cry from JoJo's Bizarre Adventure.

title: Detroit Smash
blurb: All Might announces his punches, a design choice My Hero Academia commits to without a shred of embarrassment. "DETROIT SMASH!" is the big one — the Symbol of Peace's signature named attack, delivered in that booming American-comic-book cadence that made him the single most fun character in the show to impersonate. It is the sound of a man deciding a fight is over. Works beautifully for anything decisive: closing a laptop, ending an argument, deleting the branch.
origin: All Might's signature attack call from My Hero Academia.

title: Super Saiyan Transformation
blurb: The Dragon Ball Z transformation roar: the long, straining, screaming power-up that turns a losing fight into a won one. This is arguably the most influential sound in shounen anime, since an entire genre of "the hero gets stronger by yelling for most of an episode" descends directly from Goku's first Super Saiyan moment on Namek. Decades later it is still the internet's default audio for going all-out, whether that means a workout montage or opening a spreadsheet with real determination.
origin: Goku's Super Saiyan transformation scream from Dragon Ball Z.

title: Light Yagami Laugh
blurb: Light Yagami's laugh from Death Note is the definitive anime villain cackle: the sound of a teenager who has just confirmed that his absurdly elaborate plan worked and cannot physically keep it inside any longer. It escalates gorgeously, from a smug private chuckle into full theatrical howling, and it has been pasted over every smug reveal on the internet for the better part of fifteen years. Keep it ready for the moment your own ridiculous scheme actually comes together.
origin: Light Yagami's triumphant laugh from Death Note.

title: Baka
blurb: "Baka!" — the tsundere's load-bearing word. It means idiot and is almost always used to mean approximately the opposite, which is a linguistic trick anime has been running for decades. It is probably the first Japanese word any anime viewer learns, and it has stayed in the meme vocabulary long after the shows that popularised it faded. Delivered here with the full flustered inflection, it is a soundboard essential for Discord servers, affectionate scolding, and telling a friend they are wrong without doing the work of explaining why.
origin: A stock anime delivery of the Japanese word for idiot.

title: Geometry Dash Level Complete
blurb: After several hundred deaths, this. The Geometry Dash level-complete chime is one of gaming's purest reward sounds — bright, brief, and wildly disproportionate to the misery required to earn it. Anyone who has ground out a demon level knows the very specific feeling of finally hearing this instead of the death sound for the four-hundredth time. RobTop's audio design is deliberately minimal, which leaves this one jingle carrying an enormous emotional load. Use it for finishing literally anything.
origin: The level-completion chime from Geometry Dash (RobTop Games).

title: Geometry Dash Secret Key
blurb: Geometry Dash hides an absurd quantity of content behind vaults, passwords and collectibles, and this is the chime that tells you a key has turned up somewhere you probably weren't supposed to be looking yet. It is a small, sparkling sound doing a big job: RobTop's whole secrets economy runs on it. Players who have never cleared a demon level still recognise this one from hunting through the Vault of Secrets. Good for any moment of entirely unearned discovery.
origin: The secret key collection sound from Geometry Dash.

title: Geometry Dash Chest Open
blurb: The chest-opening sound from Geometry Dash's treasure room: four hours of cooldown compressed into one satisfying crack, usually followed by the crushing disappointment of forty orbs and a shard you already had. It is a small masterpiece of variable-reward design — the sound is always great, the contents almost never are. Anybody who has set a phone alarm for a large chest timer knows exactly what this does to the brain. Play it whenever you open something with unwarranted optimism.
origin: The treasure room chest sound from Geometry Dash.

title: Geometry Dash Shards
blurb: Shards are Geometry Dash's grind currency and this is the tinkling collect sound that pays you for doing the grinding. It is a deliberately moreish little noise, the sort of audio feedback engineered to make a repetitive loop feel productive, and it is a large part of why players will happily replay the same map three dozen times in an evening. Drop it in whenever a genuinely tiny amount of progress deserves an outsized celebration.
origin: The shard pickup sound from Geometry Dash.

title: Cat Meow
blurb: A clean, classic cat meow — the single most useful animal sound there is. Here is the thing worth knowing before you press it: adult cats barely meow at each other at all. The entire vocabulary evolved specifically to manipulate humans, and it works. Beyond summoning somebody's pet from three rooms away, it makes a superb comedic non-answer — ask a difficult question, reply with this. Handy for videos, prank calls, and confusing your own cat, which is effective and mildly cruel.
origin: A studio recording of a domestic cat's meow.

title: Cat Purring
blurb: The low, steady rumble of a purring cat sits somewhere around 25 to 150 hertz, a frequency range researchers have tentatively linked to tissue healing — the science is unsettled, but the effect on humans is not. Purring is one of the most reliably calming sounds ever recorded. Use it for lo-fi backgrounds, sleep videos and ASMR edits, or simply leave it running as a small break from whatever else the internet is currently doing to you.
origin: A close recording of a domestic cat purring.

title: Chicken Cluck
blurb: Contented clucking from a hen going quietly about her business — the background texture of every farmyard scene ever filmed. Chickens have well over twenty distinct calls, and this is the everyday chatter one: not the alarm call, not the egg song. It is a staple for cartoon edits, farm-themed videos and passive-aggressively calling somebody a coward without using words. Also disproportionately funny when dropped into a silent moment on a work call.
origin: A field recording of a hen clucking.

title: Cow Moo
blurb: A proper deep moo, delivered with the total absence of urgency that only a cow can achieve. It is the sound every child learns before they can read, and it stubbornly refuses to stop being funny in the wrong context — which is precisely the argument for putting it on a soundboard. Cows moo largely to locate each other across a field, so treat this as an invitation. Excellent for farm videos, terrible driving, and answering anyone who says something extremely obvious.
origin: A field recording of a cow lowing.

title: Turkey Gobble
blurb: That rapid, warbling gobble is a male turkey advertising himself, and he can be heard doing it from a mile away, which explains both the volume and the confidence. It reads as Thanksgiving in audio form for American listeners and as pure absurdity for everybody else. Use it for holiday edits, for interrupting people mid-sentence, or as the world's most annoying notification tone. Genuinely one of the strangest noises any bird has ever agreed to make.
origin: A field recording of a wild turkey gobbling.

title: Screaming Goat
blurb: The screaming goat briefly took over the internet in 2013, when somebody realised goats sound uncannily like a person having an extremely bad day and started splicing them into pop songs. Taylor Swift's I Knew You Were Trouble was never the same again. The reason it lands so hard is acoustic: the bleat sits right inside the human vocal range, so your brain files it as a person before correcting itself half a second later. Still the funniest button on any animal soundboard, and it isn't close.
origin: The goat bleat behind the 2013 'screaming goat' meme wave.

title: Screaming Marmot
blurb: One of the founding memes of the modern internet: a marmot standing on a rock, mouth wide open, emitting a shriek that sounds convincingly like it has been dubbed by a man. It hasn't been — marmots really do produce that piercing alarm whistle to warn the colony about eagles overhead. The clip has been recycled through reaction videos for the better part of two decades and shows no interest in retiring. Perfect for overreacting to something extremely minor.
origin: The alarm call behind the long-running 'screaming marmot' meme.

title: Pigeon Scream
blurb: Pigeons do not, as a rule, scream, which is exactly what makes this clip so alarming and so funny. It has become a fixture of chaotic edits and bird-noise compilations: a sudden strangled shriek from an animal you had filed away as a walking bread receptacle. Deploy it when something entirely ordinary does something deeply unexpected. Works especially well laid over footage of anybody eating in public near a park bench.
origin: A pigeon distress call popularised through chaotic edit compilations.

title: Birds Chirping
blurb: Gentle morning birdsong: the ambient loop that quietly signals it is early and everything is fine. Editors use it in two completely opposite ways. Sincerely, for calm outdoor scenes, sleep tracks and meditation videos. Sarcastically, as the sound of total silence after somebody says something that lands very badly indeed — a comedy staple sitting right alongside crickets. It is also genuinely pleasant to leave running in a tab while you work, which is not something you can say about most of this site.
origin: An ambient field recording of dawn birdsong.

title: Minecraft Pig
blurb: The Minecraft pig oink, made in the same lo-fi, slightly-too-fast spirit as the rest of the game's mob audio. Pigs are Minecraft's most defenceless creature and their little snuffling grunt is disproportionately endearing, which is exactly why chat reacts so strongly whenever a streamer hits one for no reason. Ideal for Minecraft edits, farm-build montages, or narrating somebody rummaging around in a fridge at half past eleven at night.
origin: The pig mob sound from Minecraft (Mojang).

title: Horse Neigh
blurb: A full-throated horse neigh, complete with the rising whinny at the end. Horses neigh chiefly to make contact across distance, which explains why the sound carries so well and why it functions so beautifully as an interruption noise. It has been a comedy staple since the radio era: play it after a bad pun, over a slow-motion entrance, or any time somebody says something that deserves to be greeted by livestock rather than by people.
origin: A field recording of a horse whinnying.

title: Rubber Duck Squeak
blurb: The squeak of a rubber duck — a sound with a surprisingly serious second career in software engineering, where rubber duck debugging means explaining your broken code out loud to a bath toy until you hear the flaw yourself. It works, annoyingly often. Outside of that it is simply the perfect comedy squeak: light, silly, and impossible to take seriously for even a moment. Good for cartoon edits, bath-time videos, and punctuating your own bad decisions.
origin: A squeeze recording of a classic rubber bath duck.

title: Screaming Chicken
blurb: The rubber screaming chicken is a squeeze toy engineered for precisely one purpose, which is to make an unbearable noise. It has been a slapstick prop for decades, it drives dogs to genuine distraction, and it remains the fastest available method of ruining the atmosphere in any room. Mechanically the sound is just a reed being badly abused. Use responsibly — though nobody in recorded history has ever used a screaming chicken responsibly.
origin: A recording of the classic rubber screaming chicken toy.

title: Whale Talking
blurb: Whale song: long, mournful, weirdly musical calls that travel enormous distances through deep water. Humpback males sing structured songs that shift year on year, and whole populations adopt each new version — one of the few genuinely accepted cases of culture existing outside humans. For most listeners, though, this is simply the sound of a nature documentary, or of a certain SpongeBob character having feelings at maximum volume. Both readings are entirely welcome here.
origin: A hydrophone recording of whale song.

title: Baby Lion Roar
blurb: A lion cub attempting a roar and producing something much closer to a squeaky yawn. Lions cannot manage a proper roar until they are around two years old, so this is very much a work in progress, and it is adorable in exactly the way a full-grown roar is not. Perfect for anybody putting up a fight they cannot possibly win: a small dog, a toddler, or a colleague objecting to a decision that was finalised last week.
origin: A recording of a lion cub's early attempt at roaring.

title: Angry Monkey
blurb: Furious primate screeching — the sound of a monkey who has had quite enough and would like the whole forest to know about it. Most primate threat and alarm calls are evolutionarily designed to be as unpleasant as possible, because being ignorable would defeat the purpose, so this cuts through absolutely anything in a mix. It is a mainstay of chaotic edits and "when the group chat goes off" videos. Play it the second a conversation stops being civil.
origin: A field recording of an agitated monkey's threat call.

title: Dog Laugh
blurb: Dogs really do have a laugh — a breathy, rhythmic panting huff that behavioural researchers have recorded and even played back to shelter dogs to measurably calm them down. This clip has the classic version, and it is uncanny: it sits right on the line between an innocent pant and open mockery. Which is, inevitably, how the internet uses it. Play it whenever somebody falls over and is definitely, definitely fine.
origin: A recording of the breathy panting sound identified as canine laughter.

title: Rawr
blurb: "Rawr" is a word that mostly exists in text, delivered here out loud with full commitment. It belongs to a very specific era of the internet: scene kids, dinosaur avatars, and the phrase "rawr means I love you in dinosaur" scrawled across a MySpace profile in a font nobody could read. It has since been reclaimed as ironic playfulness, which is roughly what happens to everything eventually. Good for playful threats, cursed nostalgia, and pretending to be a very small dinosaur.
origin: The spoken version of the scene-era internet 'rawr'.

title: Gegagedigedagedago
blurb: Gegagedigedagedago began life as a nonsense chant in a Nintendo-adjacent meme and mutated into an entire subgenre, complete with its own visual language and several thousand remixes. It runs the same trick as most great brainrot: a string of syllables carrying no meaning whatsoever, delivered rhythmically enough that your brain files it as a real word anyway. Nobody can spell it. Everybody can say it. Play it to instantly identify who in the room is under sixteen.
origin: A viral nonsense chant meme spawned from Nintendo-adjacent edits.

title: The Globglogabgalab
blurb: "I am the Globglogabgalab..." — a bloated, slug-like creature from the 2011 animated film Strawinsky and the Mysterious House, an obscure production that essentially nobody watched until the internet found this one scene. The animation is deeply uncanny, the song is annoyingly catchy, and the combination gained a second life as one of the strangest memes of the late 2010s. It is a museum piece at this point. Play it and watch a very specific age bracket start swaying in unison.
origin: The Globglogabgalab's song from the 2011 film Strawinsky and the Mysterious House.

title: Quaso
blurb: Quaso is croissant, run through the same brainrot pronunciation engine that turned sigma and aura into adjectives. It arrived on a wave of TikToks in which the word is delivered with total, entirely unearned reverence for a pastry, and it stuck for the reason these things always stick: saying it correctly is impossible and saying it wrong is funnier. There is no deeper layer here, no origin story worth unpacking, no hidden meaning. There is only quaso.
origin: A TikTok brainrot pronunciation of 'croissant'.

title: Hamood Habibi
blurb: The Hamood Habibi song comes from an Arabic children's birthday video that the internet adopted wholesale, largely because the chorus is impossibly cheerful and the accompanying visuals look like they were assembled in 2006 on a budget of roughly nothing. It became a global meme with most of the people sharing it not understanding a single word — reliable proof that vibe outruns language every time. It now functions as the default birthday clip for a substantial corner of the internet.
origin: A chorus from an Arabic children's birthday song video turned meme.

title: Giga Chad
blurb: The Gigachad sting: the dramatic musical swell that accompanies every slow-motion, black-and-white, jawline-forward edit on the internet. Gigachad started as a hyper-stylised photography series and became shorthand for absurd, self-aware confidence, usually applied to something completely mundane — taking the bins out, picking the correct queue, replying "no" to an unreasonable request. The sound does all the heavy lifting. Play it immediately after any decision you would like framed as legendary.
origin: The musical sting used across Gigachad and sigma-male edits.

title: Sneaky Snitch
blurb: Kevin MacLeod's Sneaky Snitch is the pizzicato caper theme that soundtracks every act of cartoon mischief on YouTube: tiptoeing, pilfering, plotting, getting clean away with it. MacLeod released hundreds of tracks under Creative Commons licences and in the process accidentally scored an entire era of internet video, and this is far and away the most recognisable of the lot. If you have ever watched somebody do something they should not, you have heard it. Play it while doing something you should not.
origin: 'Sneaky Snitch' by Kevin MacLeod, a Creative Commons staple of YouTube video.

title: X-Files Theme
blurb: Mark Snow's whistling X-Files theme was reportedly discovered by accident, when his elbow landed on a keyboard preset and triggered an echo effect he decided to keep — one of television's great happy mistakes. A handful of notes and everyone in the room instantly knows what you are implying: that something here is deeply suspicious and possibly extraterrestrial. It is the definitive conspiracy cue, used to punctuate everything from unexplained noises upstairs to a colleague's third dentist appointment this month.
origin: Mark Snow's title theme for The X-Files (1993).

title: Oh Baby a Triple
blurb: "Oh baby, a triple!" — hollered in an old Wii bowling advert by a man whose enthusiasm exceeds the situation by several orders of magnitude. The internet extracted the line, looped it, and installed it as the standard reaction to three of anything at all. It is the purest possible form of meme: a stranger's completely genuine excitement, permanently detached from whatever caused it. Deploy it whenever something happens for the third time, however trivial.
origin: A line from a Nintendo Wii bowling advert, extracted into meme use.

title: SpongeBob Theme Song
blurb: "Are you ready, kids?" More than two decades on, the SpongeBob theme remains one of the most efficient pieces of children's television ever written: a sea-shanty call-and-response that teaches you the words on the first listen and then never, ever leaves. Series creator Stephen Hillenburg had a hand in writing it, and its cheerful pirate energy set the tone for everything that followed. Play it in a room of adults and watch every one of them answer "Aye aye, Captain!" without being asked.
origin: The opening theme of SpongeBob SquarePants (Nickelodeon, 1999).

title: Hi How Are Ya
blurb: Delivered by a passing Bikini Bottom fish with completely unshakeable confidence, "Hi, how are ya!" is one of SpongeBob's great throwaway lines — a background character who greeted his way straight into the meme canon. The appeal is entirely in the tone: relentlessly friendly, slightly too loud, and utterly uninterested in your answer. It has become a standard way to barge into a Discord call. Nobody has ever said it back.
origin: A background character's greeting from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: Imagination
blurb: SpongeBob draws a rainbow in the air with both hands and says "imagination", and two decades later it is still the internet's favourite way of describing something that does not exist. The budget for this project? Imagination. The evidence for that claim? Imagination. The clip comes from Idiot Box, an episode about the sheer joy of a cardboard box, which makes it one of the rare memes that still means roughly what it originally meant.
origin: SpongeBob's rainbow gesture from the episode 'Idiot Box' (2002).

title: 2000 Years Later
blurb: The French Narrator's time card: that lilting, faux-documentary announcement of a preposterous time jump, delivered as though it were the most natural development in the world. SpongeBob's title cards are among the most quoted gags in animation history, and this is the largest of them by some margin. Use it to acknowledge that you have now been staring at the same email for considerably longer than anybody would consider reasonable.
origin: The French Narrator's time card from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: Eww Brother Eww
blurb: "Ewww, brother! Ewww!" — the horrified nasal shriek from one of TikTok's most-replayed animated shorts, in which one sibling reacts to another with rapidly escalating disgust. It works because the delivery is so wildly disproportionate to anything actually happening on screen, and that gap is the entire joke. The clip spread across Shorts, Reels and Roblox edits within weeks. Play it when somebody tells you, unprompted, what they had for lunch.
origin: A line from a viral TikTok animated short about two brothers.

title: Dexter's Laboratory Theme
blurb: Frantic, brassy and faintly Eastern European, the Dexter's Laboratory theme sounded like nothing else on Cartoon Network in 1996. Genndy Tartakovsky's show about a boy genius with an unplaceable accent and a secret lab behind a bookcase ran on precisely that energy, and the title sequence establishes the entire premise in about eight seconds. It is a pure, uncut hit of nineties cartoon nostalgia. Play it just before doing something ill-advised in a garage.
origin: The title theme from Dexter's Laboratory (Cartoon Network, 1996).

title: Gravity Falls Theme
blurb: Brad Breeck's Gravity Falls theme is mysterious, a little rickety, and stuffed with the same secrets as the show itself — including a whispered cryptogram at the end that fans spent years decoding frame by frame. Alex Hirsch built a series in which every background hid something, and the title sequence was the first puzzle you were handed. It has become one of the most beloved cartoon themes of the 2010s. Play it whenever something around here does not quite add up.
origin: Brad Breeck's opening theme for Gravity Falls (Disney, 2012).

title: Doofenshmirtz Evil Incorporated
blurb: "DOOFENSHMIRTZ EVIL INCORPORATED!" is the greatest jingle in children's television, sung by an entire chorus for a man whose evil schemes have never once worked. The comic engine of Phineas and Ferb is Heinz Doofenshmirtz taking himself completely seriously while being completely ridiculous, and the theme announces it fresh every single episode. It is the ideal sound for entering a room with unearned menace, or for naming any project that is definitely going to fail.
origin: Dr Doofenshmirtz's building jingle from Phineas and Ferb.

title: Peppa Pig Theme
blurb: The Peppa Pig intro, with its snorts, its bouncing strings and its cast introducing themselves one by one. To small children it is the finest television ever made; to their parents it is a sound that arrives roughly four hundred times a week and never fully leaves the house. It has also become a full internet meme in its own right, remixed into everything from drill tracks to horror edits. Play it in any room containing a toddler and observe the effect immediately.
origin: The opening theme of Peppa Pig (Astley Baker Davies, 2004).

title: Homer D'oh
blurb: "D'oh!" was improvised by Dan Castellaneta on the spot, because the script simply said "annoyed grunt" and he needed something shorter. It is now an entry in the Oxford English Dictionary. Homer Simpson has been making this noise since 1989 and it remains the most efficient way ever devised to express the thought "I have just made a mistake I could clearly see coming". Play it for stubbed toes, emails sent three seconds too early, and plans that collapse on contact with reality.
origin: Homer Simpson's catchphrase from The Simpsons, improvised by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Bass Drop
blurb: The drop: that engineered moment where a build-up finally releases and the low end arrives all at once. It is the backbone of every hype edit on the internet and the standard punctuation mark for reveals, transformations and slow-motion walk-ins. Producers spend an unreasonable amount of effort on the two seconds immediately before it, because the silence is what makes the impact land at all. Best used sparingly, and at a volume that makes somebody check their speakers.
origin: A generic EDM-style bass drop used across meme and hype edits.

title: TV Static
blurb: Analogue television static — the fuzzy grey snow that filled the screen back when a channel had nothing left to give you. A small fraction of that noise was genuinely cosmic microwave background radiation left over from the Big Bang, which is a fantastic thing to tell people at parties. These days it mostly signals horror: dead channels, cursed tapes, and things standing just outside the frame. Reach for it for glitch transitions, found-footage edits, or the precise moment a scene goes wrong.
origin: Untuned analogue television static.

title: Balloon Pop
blurb: A single sharp balloon burst — a sound occupying a strange position in the human nervous system, because everybody flinches even when they watched it coming. That makes it genuinely useful: comedic for a deflating moment, startling as a jump cut, and perfect for punctuating any celebration that is about to go badly wrong. Party planners and horror editors reach for the same clip, which tells you something about both professions.
origin: A close recording of a party balloon bursting.

title: Door Slam
blurb: A heavy door slammed hard: the full stop of sound effects. Nothing else ends a scene so decisively — an argument, an exit, a flat refusal to continue the conversation. Sitcoms have used it as a punchline for decades, while horror uses it to tell you that something is now in the room with you, or alternatively that you are now completely alone. Play it when you want the last word without having to say anything at all.
origin: A recording of a heavy door being slammed shut.

title: Taser Zap
blurb: The crackling electrical arc of a stun device: a nasty, snapping buzz that anyone who has ever watched an action film recognises immediately. It has become the standard effect for anything electric going wrong — shorted wiring, malfunctioning robots, science-fiction weapons and cartoon shocks alike. Editors love it because it is short, aggressive, and cuts straight through a busy mix with no processing required. Use it when a scene needs to end abruptly and a little painfully.
origin: A recording of an electrical stun device arcing.

title: Cartoon Boing
blurb: The classic springy boing — the sound of a character rebounding off something they had no business rebounding off. It descends directly from the golden age of Warner Bros. and MGM shorts, where sound editors built an entire language of exaggerated physics out of stretched springs, slide whistles and whatever was lying around the foley room. Nothing signals "do not take this seriously" faster. Perfect for pratfalls, double-takes, and anything that needs to bounce.
origin: A classic cartoon spring effect in the Warner Bros. foley tradition.
